user_history.review_text:
High-end lenses can be so expensive. Just look at the Leica Noctilux, for example. Go ahead, google it…But even Fuji’s own 2.0 weather resistant line of lenses can be hundreds and hundreds of dollars. This leads a lot of photographers to acquire vintage glass, which can often be found for reasonable prices, but come with their own set of problems. Most old lenses need servicing and can end malfunctioning if you don’t take care of them.

Companies like TTArtisan have been popping up to provide new lenses that are affordable but also have the vintage charm without any of the quirks of using a 50+ year old lens. This lens in particular looks beautiful on Fujifilm’s latest X-Pro3. It’s worth noting that this is a fully manual lens. This means no auto focusing capabilities and no auto exposure capabilities. But that’s part of the fun! The focus turns very smoothly and the aperture clicks into place with satisfying feedback. And you’ll never mistake one for the other thanks to the grippy striped focus ring that protrudes much more distinctly from the lens allowing you to grip it with ease.

Be sure to select the setting in your camera so that you can “take photos without lens” because the camera’s computer will not know there’s a lens attached due to the lack of autofocus and auto exposure contact points. From there, your camera will tell you that it’s shooting at an F0, and it becomes up to you to set the SS and ISO within the camera and then manually set the aperture and focus.

I recommend turning on a focus assist of some kind, like peaking. That way you’re never guessing whether your shot will be sharp.

Essentially, all of my work was erased and I am still unable to access any of that footage–so disappointing!

I should have read the reviews before trying this memory card out– it turns out that customer service is just as unreliable as the reviews state. When I tried to get ahold of them, you chat with a bot most of the time who tells you that you need to update or restart your device. They never actually offer any advice and I’ve yet to figure out a way to actually contact a real person. There are hardly any videos online that can troubleshoot this problem which makes me think that it is just a hardware issue with the actual chip.

Overall, if you’re looking for something that actually works to store data, look elsewhere or try to find some kind of alternate instruction.

user_history.review_text:
Once upon a time, USB, WiFi and Ethernet print servers were all the rage. But that was long ago, when Centroncs parallel and occasionally serial interfaces were the standard ways to communicate with printers (and usually dot matrix printers, to boot!) and people wanted to modernize without buying a new printer. Sometimes you just loved a printer and didn't want to let it go: I had an Epson Color Stylus 1520 that I kept alive for years because of its versatility.

Today, it's the rare printer that doesn't have USB and WiFi interfaces, so the need for external print servers has greatly diminished. But there are still some USB printers that people would like to add to their WiFi networks and this device will allow them to do just that.

First, this is not a network print server, It is for single device.

Second, take a deep breath before you try to install this, count to ten and repeat to yourself "This is not necessarily a plug-and-play device! This is not necessarily a plug-and-play device! This is not necessarily a plug-and-play device!"
You might even consider not only downloading the 23 page manual, but carefully reading it as well. (It's mostly pictures!)

If you are running Windows 8, 8.1 or 10, you very much want to read the FAQs on the StarTech website. Doing so will save your sanity and make for an easy installation.

Many people don't realize how bad the good old days were when it came to installing printers. You're going to get a taste of it here.

Relax. Read the manual and the FAQs and don't explode when you see this isn't quite the plug-and-play you're used to.

The payoff for your patience will be a printer that you can now dependably access via WiFi.

Once installed, this print server works well.

Jerry

This is a rather nice power supply, and while there are just a few reviews here, you'll find a few professional reviews at places like Johnny Guru, Tom's Hardware, and the like. As they discovered, this is a rather nice power supply.

Unboxing the unit was similar to my Corsair AX series PSU, with a nice bag for all of the cables and a slightly elongated black cube. There are a ton of cables, and while I'd appreciate them being less stiff, it's all par for the course. The length is also pretty typical. Enough for an ATX mid tower or cube, more than you'd like for a ITX box and probably not enough for an old school full tower. Being modular and from a company as popular as Corsair, replacement options are available. I do wish, and this applies to my Silverstone PSUs as well, that the receptacles for the cables on the PSU were easier to identify and easier to insert. It's really hard to do once everything is in place. I've dreaded adding a 2.5" drive in other systems just because I didn't want to add a sata power cable, and this is no different. I do appreciate the semi recessed plugs, as it does make the somewhat large PSU not any bigger. One last cable gripe, which again isn't unique to Corsair, the SATA power connectors down't work well for 2.5" drives mounted on a case floor or wall. I have two cases like this and the connectors with wires going in and out just don't work well so close to the floor or wall. I'd say this is just as much of a case design issue as anything, but this PSU (as well as others I've used) aren't helping.

In use I've found my Skylake system to be remarkably stable with all voltages showing well within tolerances. That should be no surprises, as I saw outstanding results in measured tests at jonnyguru.com. While I kept the fan in hybrid mode, it hard is ever noticeable, whether it's off or simply running slowly, this is a very quiet PSU. I also didn't notice any coil whine or other noises.

I wholeheartedly recommend this PSU, but I would advise folks to consider the length. This is a rather long 750w power supply. Otherwise it has all of the usual features, some of the nice to have ones, and it does so much so well.

user_history.review_text:
So on the SSD version of this drive, which only comes in a 512GB model, the casing is aluminum, and it's black with a green "stripe" around the sides. I honestly don't understand why they chose a bright, garish green for this. Nothing on either Xbox One console (original and S) is this color. The original Xbox One is black and chrome. The Xbox One-S is white and black. No weird green anywhere, unless you count the boot screen when you first turn the Xbox on.

That said, the case is still nice (oh, and make sure you peel off the clear plastic from around the green part; It's not meant to stay on and it might contribute to trapping heat.) Like many other external drives of this sort, it lacks any sort of rubber feet, so it's just laying flat on whatever surface you choose to place it upon. Since this would usually be the Xbox One itself, it has the potential for scratching, and as that's a smooth surface it also slides around a bit if you nudge the cable or drive. I solved this problem by adding some silicon bumpers - [[ASIN:B01N417DBE Homder 172-Piece Transparent Self-Adhesive Bumper Pads Combo Pack Noise Dampening,Furniture Pads for Cabinets, Small Furniture, Picture Frames, Cutting Boards and More(Round,Square)]] - to the bottom.

As for the drive itself. It's fast! It's very easy to install. Just plug it in AFTER the Xbox One is on and running and then follow the prompts, letting the Xbox One format the drive for storage (not media!) -- Since the USB 3.0 port is faster than the internal SATA on the Xbox One, this loads games a lot faster than games installed on the internal hard drive. It also means you can buy that cheaper Xbox One and rely on this external storage without fussing over having more space built-in. You actually come out on top with the external storage versus internal storage!

Once you have it installed, it will function just like the internal drive (only faster!) and you can have games automatically installed to that drive from that point onward. But what about game already on your internal hard drive? Easy. Go to the game's icon, press the (=) button on your controller, and choose "manage game", then "move all" and pick the new external hard drive. Easy!

Sadly, at this point Microsoft has NOT come up with a way to pick a bunch of games and move them all at once. You have to pick each game individually and move them one by one. You can keep picking games to move and the Xbox One will queue them for moving, but there's no way to select a bunch at once instead of selecting one by one.

Moving games to your new SSD doesn't take much time, really, when you consider the sizes we're dealing with here. Once you've done it, you'll see a dramatic shortening of load times, and of course you'll have freed up a lot of space on the internal hard drive.

You can also take the external SSD over to a friend's house and play the games on his or her Xbox One, provided you log in with your Gamertag. If your Xbox ever dies or (gasp!) gets stolen, and you still have the external hard drive, all your games are backed up and ready to go when you plug into a new Xbox One and log in with your Gamertag. If course, you could always re-download all the games (unless you bought all your games on disc, in which case the thief probably took those, too, and you're out of luck) but this is much faster! It will save you a day's worth of downloading and a lot of Internet bandwidth when migrating to a new console.

I can't say enough nice things about having an external SSD on the Xbox One. Frankly, I wish they'd built a small one into the console itself (along with a 6GB/s SATA port). Oh well... Maybe they'll do that with future models. Until then, this is the FASTEST way to load games on the Xbox One. Skyrim and The Witcher 3 are a delight on an external USB 3.0 SSD. Load times are a fraction of what they were on the internal drive.

Yes, you could technically get another external SSD without the Xbox branding and it would probably work. This one's just a touch easier (it will be recognized by the Xbox One without any extra work on your part; Some other SSDs will require you to do some initializing or formatting on a PC) and has the XBOX logo on the casing. Is that worth the price difference? That all depends on you. Are you tech savvy or do you just want to plug it in and have it work? If you're decent with computers, then you might want to save the money and get a different Seagate drive and go through any extra steps that may be required. If you're giving this as a gift or aren't interested in fiddling with the PC, then the Seagate Game Drive is packaged and ready to go for your Xbox One, and it works right out of the box.

Of course, the only real down-side to going with an SSD is that you have less storage than with a traditional hard drive. It's up to you if you want the benefit of speed, or if you just want a lot more storage space. In my setup, I have a 2TB external hard drive connected for storage of all the games I'm currently not playing (but will, eventually), and the SSD in place as my "currently playing" drive so that I get the benefit of faster load times. I just move games back and forth as needed, with all my favorite games permanently living on the SSD.

My advice? If you're getting all those great Games With Gold and need extra storage space, I'd probably recommend a large hard drive as your first choice, just so you have a place to keep all those free games until you're ready to play them. Grab the SSD for the speed bonus after you secure the larger space. 512GB is a lot, but 2TB is better if extra space is more of a concern than extra speed.

Original review of Five stars. Really, I'd give it more like 4 and a half stars because that green stripe is silly and the price is a little high for the Xbox One version versus a standard SSD, but since Amazon doesn't do half-stars, I'll be generous and round up because this really is a nice SSD in a decent package.

UPDATE 06/2017 - Well, after a hard reboot of my Xbox One console, this SSD has completely failed a very short time after I first got it. The Xbox One doesn't recognize it, and three different PCs didn't recognize it. Partition programs didn't see it, even when the drive was put onto a different SATA connector, and well... It's dead. Totally dead. All my games were lost and had to be re-downloaded. I'm pretty bummed. An SSD should be able to handle an Xbox One having the power cut off. There was no surge (it's on a nice surge protector, anyway) and there was no impact or damage. It just failed when I did a hard reboot and that was that.

So I'm amending my review to reflect my experience with the failure of this SSD. Considering the price and focused Xbox One intentions, it should have been able to handle a normal hard reboot, and it didn't. Your mileage may vary, but my experience has been frustrating and disappointing. It was good while it lasted... it's just too bad it doesn't seem to last.
user_history.review_title: Failed within a few months after a reboot.
